title: Set iron condor strikes with the market's implied move
summary: Do not pick iron condor strikes at random. Use the market's own implied expected move: here Amazon is priced to move about plus or minus $25 over 28 days, so the short strikes sit $25 below and above the market with $25 wide wings. The trade is a bet that implied volatility overstates the move Amazon will actually make.

params.label: Excess drift over rate
params.help: Your view of annual return above the risk-free rate. Zero = the market view; EV is then about zero.

steps.caption: Implied volatility turns into a price distribution. Watch it widen as the days to expiry grow from 1 to 28.
The one standard deviation band is the market's implied move: about plus or minus $25 for Amazon over 28 days.
Two standard deviations cover about 95% of outcomes under the model. Tails beyond that still happen.
Short strikes at the implied move, $25 wings: the green zone between the short strikes keeps the credit.
Breakevens sit a little outside the short strikes, shifted out by the credit received.
At fair implied volatility the expected value is near zero. The edge exists only if realized volatility comes in below implied.

takeaways: Expected move = price x IV x square root of (days / 365). Use it to place the short strikes.
An iron condor is a short volatility bet: it wins when the stock moves less than the market priced.
Selling volatility into an earnings release breaks a common rule; the speaker flags this example as an exception.
caveats: The example straddles an earnings release. The owner's X06 rule says do not pre-position for event moves.

backtest.note: Short strikes near 16 delta (about one implied move), wings near 5 delta, 28 days to expiry.
